# ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Gap Analysis — Mid-Size Finance Firm

---

## 1. Prioritized Gap Analysis Checklist

The logic here: **Must-have** items are either mandatory clauses (4–10) or Annex A controls that your regulator, auditor, or risk profile will scrutinize first in a finance/customer-data context. **Nice-to-have** items strengthen your posture but won't block certification in year one.

### Mandatory Clauses (4–10) — all required, no exceptions

| Ref | Requirement | Your current state | Gap? | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4.1–4.2 | Context, interested parties (regulators, customers, board) | Informal | Yes | Must-have |
| 4.3 | ISMS scope document | None | Yes | Must-have |
| 5.1–5.3 | Leadership commitment, policy, roles | Partial policies exist | Yes | Must-have |
| 6.1.2 | Formal risk assessment methodology | Informal risk register | Yes | Must-have |
| 6.1.3 | Risk treatment plan + Statement of Applicability | None | Yes | Must-have |
| 6.2 | Information security objectives | None documented | Yes | Must-have |
| 7.1–7.5 | Resources, awareness, documented information control | Partial | Yes | Must-have |
| 8.1–8.3 | Operational planning, risk treatment execution | None | Yes | Must-have |
| 9.1–9.3 | Monitoring, internal audit, management review | None formal | Yes | Must-have |
| 10.1–10.2 | Nonconformity, continual improvement | None formal | Yes | Must-have |

### Annex A Controls Gap Analysis

Annex A (2022) has 93 controls across four themes: Organizational (37), People (8), Physical (14), Technological (34). I've focused on the gaps most relevant to your profile.

**Organizational controls**

| Control | Description | Your state | Gap | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5.1 | Information security policies | Partial (access, incident) | Gaps in scope and review cycle | Must-have |
| 5.9 | Asset inventory | CMDB for major assets only | Incomplete — cloud/SaaS assets missing | Must-have |
| 5.10 | Acceptable use | Unknown | Likely missing | Must-have |
| 5.12–5.13 | Classification and labelling | Unknown | Likely missing for customer data | Must-have |
| 5.15 | Access control policy | Partial | Needs formalizing and linking to Azure AD | Must-have |
| 5.19–5.22 | Supplier security | Contracts exist, no program | Significant gap — finance auditors will probe this | Must-have |
| 5.23 | Cloud services security | None formal | Gap — Azure, O365, Salesforce all in scope | Must-have |
| 5.24–5.28 | Incident management (IS-specific) | ITIL incidents exist | Needs IS-specific classification and reporting | Must-have |
| 5.29–5.30 | Business continuity / ICT readiness | Backups exist | No formal BCP/ISCP tested | Must-have |
| 5.31–5.36 | Legal, compliance, privacy | Partial | Finance regulation mapping needed | Must-have |
| 5.7 | Threat intelligence | Outsourced SOC | Formalize intake and response loop | Nice-to-have |
| 5.8 | IS in project management | Unknown | Usually weak in first-year ISMS | Nice-to-have |

**People controls**

| Control | Description | Your state | Gap | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6.1–6.2 | Screening, terms and conditions | HR-owned, likely exists | Confirm and document | Must-have |
| 6.3 | IS awareness and training | Informal | No annual programme or tracking | Must-have |
| 6.4–6.5 | Disciplinary process, post-employment | HR-owned | Confirm and cross-reference IS policy | Nice-to-have |
| 6.8 | IS event reporting (by staff) | Informal | Needs a clear reporting channel | Must-have |

**Physical controls**

| Control | Description | Your state | Gap | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 7.1–7.4 | Physical perimeters, entry, office/desk security | Likely partial | Formal register of secure areas needed | Must-have |
| 7.6 | Working in secure areas | Unknown | Often overlooked | Nice-to-have |
| 7.9–7.10 | Clear desk, storage media | Informal | Policy and spot-check evidence needed | Must-have |
| 7.13–7.14 | Equipment maintenance, secure disposal | SCCM/Intune partial | Disposal records often missing | Must-have |

**Technological controls — highest gap area for your environment**

| Control | Description | Your state | Gap | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8.2 | Privileged access management | Azure AD, some controls | No formal PAM process or review cycle | Must-have |
| 8.3 | Information access restriction | Azure AD / RBAC | Needs documented role matrix | Must-have |
| 8.5 | Secure authentication | MFA likely partial | MFA coverage needs documenting | Must-have |
| 8.6–8.7 | Capacity management, malware protection | Partial | Formal capacity plan missing | Nice-to-have |
| 8.8 | Technical vulnerability management | SCCM/Intune patching | No formal SLA, remediation tracking, or scanning for cloud assets | Must-have |
| 8.9 | Configuration management | CMDB partial | Cloud configs and baselines not covered | Must-have |
| 8.10 | Information deletion | Unknown | Customer data deletion process needed (also regulatory) | Must-have |
| 8.11 | Data masking | Unknown | Likely needed for finance/customer data | Must-have |
| 8.15–8.16 | Logging and monitoring | Splunk + SOC | Good base — needs formal log retention policy and review SLA | Must-have |
| 8.20–8.22 | Network security, segregation, filtering | Unknown | Hybrid network diagram and segmentation docs needed | Must-have |
| 8.23 | Web filtering | Unknown | Document or implement | Nice-to-have |
| 8.24 | Cryptography | Unknown | Encryption-at-rest and in-transit policy needed | Must-have |
| 8.25–8.31 | Secure development | Unknown | If no in-house dev, can be excluded with justification | Depends on scope |
| 8.32 | Change management | ITIL change exists | Good — needs IS review step added | Must-have |
| 8.34 | Protection of IS during audit | None | Often missed | Nice-to-have |

---

## 2. Highest-Priority Controls Mapped to Your Tools — with Audit Evidence Examples

These are the controls auditors hit hardest in finance environments, matched to what you already have.

### 5.9 — Asset Inventory
**Your tools:** CMDB, Azure portal, Intune, Salesforce admin console, O365 admin center

What you need to do: extend your CMDB to cover cloud VMs, SaaS accounts, and data assets, not just on-prem major assets. Create an owner field and a data classification field.

**Audit evidence you can realistically provide:**
- An exported asset register (Excel or CMDB report) covering on-prem, Azure VMs, and licensed SaaS accounts with owner and classification columns
- A documented process for how new assets get added (e.g., triggered by Azure subscription tag policy or Intune enrollment)
- A periodic review record showing the register was reviewed in the last 12 months

---

### 8.2 / 8.3 / 8.5 — Privileged Access, Access Restriction, Secure Authentication
**Your tools:** Azure AD / Entra ID, Intune, potentially PIM (Privileged Identity Management)

What you need to do: document your RBAC role matrix, enable and evidence MFA across all users (especially privileged), run and retain quarterly access reviews, and enable just-in-time access for admin roles via Azure PIM if not already done.

**Audit evidence you can realistically provide:**
- Azure AD access review reports (run from Entra Identity Governance — these are exportable)
- MFA registration status report showing % coverage, exported from Entra
- A role matrix document mapping job titles to Azure AD groups and permissions
- PIM activation logs showing privileged access is time-bound
- A leavers/movers process document with example tickets showing access was removed within your SLA

---

### 8.8 — Technical Vulnerability Management
**Your tools:** SCCM/Intune for patching, Splunk for logs, outsourced SOC/MDR

What you need to do: formalize a vulnerability management policy with patch SLAs by severity (e.g., critical: 48h, high: 7 days, medium: 30 days). Extend scanning to Azure workloads (Microsoft Defender for Cloud gives you this). Document what happens when a patch can't be applied (risk acceptance).

**Audit evidence you can realistically provide:**
- Intune/SCCM compliance reports showing patch status by device, exportable on a schedule
- Microsoft Defender for Cloud secure score and recommendation exports for Azure assets
- A vulnerability management policy with SLAs signed by the CISO/IT director
- A risk acceptance log for patches that couldn't be deployed in SLA (even one or two examples show the process works)
- SOC/MDR monthly reports showing vulnerability findings and remediation tracking

---

### 5.19–5.22 / 5.23 — Supplier Security and Cloud Services
**Your tools:** existing vendor contracts, Azure, O365, Salesforce

What you need to do: build a supplier register, tier your suppliers by risk (Azure and Salesforce handle customer data — they're tier 1), document what security assurances you've obtained (SOC 2 reports, ISO 27001 certs, Microsoft shared responsibility model), and add security review clauses to new contracts.

**Audit evidence you can realistically provide:**
- A supplier register with risk tier, data processed, contractual security clauses column, and last-review date
- Downloaded SOC 2 Type II reports for Salesforce and Microsoft (available via their trust portals)
- Microsoft's shared responsibility matrix for your Azure workloads, annotated to show your side
- Meeting minutes or email trail showing annual supplier security reviews
- A supplier onboarding checklist for new vendors

---

### 5.24–5.28 — Information Security Incident Management
**Your tools:** ITIL incident process, outsourced SOC/MDR, Splunk

What you need to do: overlay an IS-specific classification scheme (security event → security incident → major incident) on your existing ITIL process. Define what triggers regulatory notification (in finance this is often mandatory within 24–72h depending on jurisdiction). Document the SOC escalation path.

**Audit evidence you can realistically provide:**
- An IS incident classification procedure document (can be an annex to your existing incident policy)
- SOC/MDR escalation runbook or SLA document
- A sample incident log (even from a tabletop exercise) showing classification, response, and closure
- A post-incident review record for any real or simulated security incident
- Evidence of a tabletop exercise (agenda, attendees, outcomes) — auditors love this

---

### 8.15–8.16 — Logging and Monitoring
**Your tools:** Splunk, outsourced SOC/MDR

What you need to do: document log sources, retention periods (typically 12 months online, 7 years for finance), and the alert/response SLA with your SOC. Ensure logs are protected from tampering.

**Audit evidence you can realistically provide:**
- A log management policy covering sources, retention, and review frequency
- Splunk dashboard screenshot or export showing active log ingestion from key sources (Azure, on-prem, O365)
- SOC/MDR contract or SLA document referencing alert response times
- A sample SOC report or alert closure ticket showing end-to-end handling
- Evidence of log integrity protection (Splunk index checksums, or Azure Monitor immutable storage)

---

### 8.32 — Change Management
**Your tools:** ITIL change process

What you need to do: add an information security review step to your change advisory board (CAB) process. This doesn't need to be heavyweight — a checkbox and a named reviewer on the change record is enough for most audits.

**Audit evidence you can realistically provide:**
- Change records (from your ITSM tool) showing an IS review field populated
- CAB meeting minutes referencing security sign-off on significant changes
- A change management procedure document referencing the IS review step

---

## 3. Statement of Applicability — Template Outline

The SoA is a mandatory document (Clause 6.1.3d). It lists all 93 Annex A controls, states whether each is applicable, provides a justification, and references the implementation evidence. Here is a working structure.

---

**[Organisation Name] — Statement of Applicability**
**ISMS Reference:** [doc ref] | **Version:** 1.0 | **Date:** [date] | **Owner:** CISO / IT Director
**ISO/IEC 27001:2022 — Annex A (93 controls)**

---

**Section 1 — Document Purpose and Scope**

This SoA identifies all controls from ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A that are applicable to [Org Name]'s ISMS. The ISMS scope covers [insert scope: e.g., "the provision of financial services including customer data processing, across hybrid infrastructure comprising on-premises systems, Microsoft Azure, and SaaS platforms including Microsoft 365 and Salesforce, operated from [location(s)]"].

This document was derived from the information security risk assessment dated [date] and the risk treatment plan dated [date].

---

**Section 2 — Control Table**

The main body of the SoA is a table with one row per control. Use this column structure:

| Column | Content |
|---|---|
| Control ref | e.g., 5.9 |
| Control name | e.g., Inventory of information and other associated assets |
| Applicable? | Yes / No |
| Justification for inclusion or exclusion | e.g., "Included: organisation processes personal and financial data across hybrid environment. Asset visibility is required for risk management." Or for exclusions: "Excluded: no in-house software development undertaken." |
| Implementation status | Implemented / Partially implemented / Planned / Not started |
| Evidence reference | e.g., "Asset Register v1.2, CMDB export, Azure tag policy doc" |
| Risk treatment ref | Link to the risk or treatment in your risk register |

A few practical notes on exclusions: you can only exclude a control if it is genuinely not relevant to your context and no risk in your risk treatment plan requires it. Auditors will challenge exclusions in a finance environment, so be conservative. Secure development (8.25–8.31) is the most defensible exclusion if you truly have no in-house development.

---

**Section 3 — Summary Statistics**

Include a simple count: total controls applicable, total excluded, total fully implemented, partially implemented, and planned. This shows the auditor you have a handle on your programme.

---

**Section 4 — Review and Approval**

| Role | Name | Signature | Date |
|---|---|---|---|
| ISMS Owner | | | |
| IT Director / CISO | | | |
| Management Representative | | | |

Review frequency: annually, or following significant changes to scope, risk profile, or the standard.

---

Given your 12-month target, a rough phasing that fits your existing capabilities would be:

# ISO/IEC 27001:2022 — 12-Month Project Plan & Templates

---

## Part 1: 12-Month Project Plan

### How to read this plan

Owners are abbreviated: **IL** = IT Lead, **SEC** = Security/CISO, **HR** = HR Manager, **LGL** = Legal/Compliance, **MGT** = Senior Management. Effort estimates are realistic for a 250-person firm running this alongside business-as-usual. Where a task says "ongoing" it means it needs a recurring calendar entry, not constant active work.

---

### Phase 1 — Foundation (Months 1–3)
*Goal: ISMS exists on paper, risk assessment complete, SoA drafted, executive buy-in secured.*

| # | Task | Owner | Effort estimate | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.1 | Appoint ISMS Owner and project sponsor | MGT + SEC | 1 day | Without named ownership, nothing else sticks. CISO or IT Director is typical. |
| 1.2 | Define and document ISMS scope (Clause 4.3) | SEC + IL | 2–3 days | Cover hybrid environment explicitly: on-prem, Azure, O365, Salesforce. Geographic scope matters for finance regulators. |
| 1.3 | Context analysis — internal/external issues, interested parties (Clause 4.1–4.2) | SEC + LGL + MGT | 2 days | Interview department heads. Interested parties include regulator, customers, auditors, board. |
| 1.4 | Obtain formal management sign-off on ISMS scope and charter | MGT | 1 day (meeting) | Get this in writing — it's Clause 5.1 evidence and sets the tone. |
| 1.5 | Conduct formal information security risk assessment (Clause 6.1.2) | SEC + IL | 5–8 days | Use a simple likelihood/impact matrix. Cover assets, threats, vulnerabilities. Document methodology first. |
| 1.6 | Produce risk treatment plan (Clause 6.1.3) | SEC | 3 days | Maps each risk to a treatment (mitigate/accept/transfer/avoid) and links to Annex A controls. |
| 1.7 | Draft Statement of Applicability v1.0 | SEC + IL | 3–4 days | Use the template in Part 2. At this stage, status column will be mostly "planned." |
| 1.8 | Draft core policy library (see list below) | SEC + LGL | 10–15 days total | Assign one policy per week. Policies don't need to be long — 2–4 pages each is fine. |
| 1.9 | Establish ISMS document control process (Clause 7.5) | SEC + IL | 1 day | A SharePoint folder with version control and access restrictions is sufficient. |
| 1.10 | Set information security objectives (Clause 6.2) | SEC + MGT | 1 day | 3–5 measurable objectives. E.g., "95% of critical patches applied within 48h by Q3." |

**Core policy library for Phase 1 (10–12 documents):**
Information Security Policy (top-level), Acceptable Use, Access Control, Incident Management (IS overlay), Asset Management, Vulnerability Management, Cryptography, Supplier Security, Data Classification, Clear Desk/Screen, Business Continuity/ICT Readiness, Log Management.

**Phase 1 milestone:** Risk assessment signed off, SoA v1.0 approved by management, core policies drafted. *Target: end of month 3.*

---

### Phase 2 — Control Implementation (Months 4–6)
*Goal: Must-have Annex A gaps closed, evidence generation begins, tools configured.*

| # | Task | Owner | Effort estimate | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2.1 | Extend asset register to cover Azure, SaaS, and data assets | IL | 3–5 days | Export from Azure portal, Intune, O365 admin, Salesforce. Merge into master register with owner and classification fields. |
| 2.2 | Implement data classification scheme and label critical data stores | SEC + IL | 3 days | Four tiers typical: Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted. Apply to SharePoint, Azure storage, Salesforce. |
| 2.3 | Build supplier register and tier suppliers by risk | LGL + SEC | 2–3 days | Start with vendors touching customer data. Collect SOC 2 / ISO certs for Tier 1 suppliers (Microsoft, Salesforce). |
| 2.4 | Add security review step to CAB/change process | IL | 1 day | Add an IS review field and named reviewer to your change record template. Update CAB terms of reference. |
| 2.5 | Formalize vulnerability management process | IL + SEC | 3–4 days | Define patch SLAs, enable Defender for Cloud on Azure, create remediation tracking in your ITSM. |
| 2.6 | Run access review — all privileged accounts | IL + SEC | 2–3 days | Export from Entra ID. Review admin roles, service accounts, shared accounts. Document and retain results. |
| 2.7 | Document and evidence MFA coverage | IL | 1 day | Export MFA registration report from Entra. Identify and remediate gaps. Set a 100% target for privileged users. |
| 2.8 | Enable and document Azure PIM for privileged roles | IL | 2 days | Just-in-time activation for Global Admin, Subscription Owner. Activation logs become audit evidence. |
| 2.9 | Overlay IS incident classification on ITIL process | SEC + IL | 2 days | Define event/incident/major incident thresholds. Add regulatory notification trigger and timelines. Brief SOC. |
| 2.10 | Produce log management policy and validate Splunk coverage | IL + SEC | 2–3 days | Document log sources, retention (12 months online minimum, check your regulatory requirement), review SLA with SOC. |
| 2.11 | Conduct supplier security review for Tier 1 vendors | LGL + SEC | 2 days | Review Microsoft and Salesforce shared responsibility docs. Download their latest SOC 2 reports. File and date-stamp. |
| 2.12 | Physical security — document secure areas, review access logs, clear desk policy launch | IL + MGT | 2 days | Walk the floor. Register server rooms, comms rooms. Brief all staff on clear desk. |
| 2.13 | Launch IS awareness training programme | HR + SEC | 3–5 days to set up | Use an e-learning platform or build in your LMS. Must be annual and tracked. Completion rates are audit evidence. |
| 2.14 | Confirm HR screening and IS clauses in employment contracts | HR + LGL | 2 days | Verify pre-employment checks are documented. Confirm NDA and IS responsibilities are in contracts or acceptable use sign-off. |
| 2.15 | Document network architecture and segmentation | IL | 3 days | Hybrid network diagram showing on-prem, Azure VNets, SaaS connections, firewall boundaries. This gets audited. |
| 2.16 | Document cryptography controls (encryption at rest and in transit) | IL + SEC | 2 days | Azure storage encryption settings, TLS policy, BitLocker/Intune device encryption status report. |
| 2.17 | Document and test backup and recovery | IL | 2 days | Evidence backup jobs running, test a restore, record the result. This is a finance auditor favourite. |

**Phase 2 milestone:** All must-have Annex A gaps have an owner, a task, and evidence starting to accumulate. Asset register, supplier register, and access review complete. *Target: end of month 6.*

---

### Phase 3 — Embedding and Evidence (Months 7–9)
*Goal: Processes are running, evidence is being collected routinely, internal audit conducted.*

| # | Task | Owner | Effort estimate | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3.1 | Run quarterly access review (second cycle) | IL + SEC | 1 day | Make this a recurring calendar event. Retain each cycle's output as evidence. |
| 3.2 | Run tabletop incident response exercise | SEC + IL + MGT | Half day | Scenario-based (e.g., ransomware, data breach). Document attendees, scenario, findings, and actions. Auditors love this. |
| 3.3 | Conduct internal audit against ISO 27001 (Clauses 4–10 and Annex A) | SEC or external consultant | 5–8 days | If you don't have internal audit capability, hire a consultant. This is a Clause 9.2 requirement and surfaces gaps before the certification body does. |
| 3.4 | Log and track nonconformities from internal audit | SEC | Ongoing | A simple register (finding, severity, owner, due date, closure date) satisfies Clause 10.1. |
| 3.5 | Conduct first formal management review (Clause 9.3) | MGT + SEC + IL | Half day (meeting) | Agenda must cover: audit results, risk status, objectives progress, incidents, supplier performance, resource needs. Minute it formally. |
| 3.6 | Update SoA to reflect actual implementation status | SEC | 1–2 days | Move controls from "planned" to "implemented" or "partially implemented" with evidence references. |
| 3.7 | Complete IS awareness training — first full cohort | HR + SEC | Ongoing | Chase completions. 100% is the target; document any exceptions with reason. |
| 3.8 | Run vulnerability scan across full estate (on-prem + Azure) | IL + SEC | 2 days | Use Defender for Cloud plus a network scanner (Nessus, Qualys, or similar). Produce a findings report with remediation status. |
| 3.9 | Test BCP/ICT continuity plan | IL + MGT | 1 day | A tabletop test is acceptable. Document the scenario, findings, and any updates to the plan. |
| 3.10 | Review and update risk register | SEC | 1–2 days | Reflect any changes from internal audit findings, incidents, or new services onboarded. |
| 3.11 | Confirm data deletion/retention procedures are documented and working | LGL + IL | 2 days | Finance sector typically has regulatory data retention requirements. Customer data deletion process must be evidenced. |
| 3.12 | Engage certification body — Stage 1 audit (document review) | SEC + MGT | 1 day prep + audit | Stage 1 is a desk review. The CB checks your ISMS documentation. Book this 6–8 weeks in advance. |

**Phase 3 milestone:** Internal audit complete, nonconformities logged and being remediated, management review minuted, Stage 1 audit booked. *Target: end of month 9.*

---

### Phase 4 — Pre-Certification and Certification (Months 10–12)
*Goal: Stage 1 findings resolved, Stage 2 audit passed, certificate issued.*

| # | Task | Owner | Effort estimate | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4.1 | Remediate Stage 1 findings | SEC + IL + relevant owners | 2–4 weeks | Stage 1 will likely surface documentation gaps and a few control weaknesses. Prioritize anything the CB flags as a potential major nonconformity. |
| 4.2 | Final SoA review and sign-off | SEC + MGT | 1 day | SoA must be current and signed before Stage 2. |
| 4.3 | Compile evidence pack | SEC + IL | 3–5 days | Organise evidence by control reference. Auditors will request samples — having a tidy folder structure saves significant time during Stage 2. |
| 4.4 | Brief all relevant staff on audit process | SEC + HR | Half day | Staff should know what the audit is, who the auditors are, what to say if approached. Authenticity matters — auditors sometimes speak to non-IT staff. |
| 4.5 | Stage 2 certification audit (on-site) | CB auditors | 2–3 days typically | Auditors will interview staff, review evidence, and test controls. Have IL and SEC available throughout. |
| 4.6 | Respond to any Stage 2 nonconformities | SEC + IL | 1–2 weeks | Minor NCs are normal and don't prevent certification if a credible corrective action plan is submitted within the CB's deadline (typically 30–90 days). |
| 4.7 | Certificate issued | CB | — | Valid for 3 years, with annual surveillance audits. |
| 4.8 | Establish ongoing ISMS calendar (surveillance readiness) | SEC | 1 day | Schedule: quarterly access reviews, annual training, annual internal audit, annual management review, annual risk review, annual supplier reviews. |

**Phase 4 milestone:** Certificate issued, ongoing ISMS calendar in place. *Target: end of month 12.*

---

### Summary Timeline View

| Phase | Months | Key milestone |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Foundation | 1–3 | Risk assessment signed off, SoA v1.0 approved, policies drafted |
| 2 — Implementation | 4–6 | Must-have gaps closed, evidence generation started |
| 3 — Embedding | 7–9 | Internal audit complete, Stage 1 audit conducted |
| 4 — Certification | 10–12 | Stage 2 audit passed, certificate issued |

---

## Part 2: Ready-to-Use Templates

Each template below is designed to be pasted directly into Word, SharePoint, or your ITSM/GRC tool. Adjust field names to match your existing tooling.

---

### Template 1 — Asset Register Entry

Paste this as a table row in your master asset register. One row per asset.

| Asset ID | AST-0042 | |

| Connected systems | Azure AD (SSO), internal CRM integration | |

**When to create a new row:** any new system, cloud service, data store, or significant physical asset. Trigger this from your onboarding or change process.

---

### Template 2 — Vulnerability Management Policy (Short-Form)

This is a one-page policy suitable as a standalone document or section within a broader security policy.

---

**Vulnerability Management Policy**
**Version:** 1.0 | **Owner:** IT Lead / CISO | **Review date:** [annual]

**Purpose.** This policy defines how [Organisation Name] identifies, assesses, and remediates technical vulnerabilities across its IT estate, including on-premises systems, Azure cloud workloads, and managed endpoints, to reduce the risk of exploitation and protect customer and financial data.

**Scope.** All IT assets within the ISMS scope, including servers, endpoints, network devices, cloud resources, and SaaS platforms where vulnerability data is available.

**Responsibilities.** The IT Lead owns the vulnerability management process. The CISO reviews remediation performance monthly. The outsourced SOC/MDR notifies the IT Lead of actively exploited vulnerabilities within their detection remit.

**Scanning.** Authenticated vulnerability scans must be conducted across all in-scope assets at minimum monthly. Cloud assets must be assessed via Microsoft Defender for Cloud or equivalent on a continuous basis. New assets must be scanned within 5 business days of provisioning.

**Remediation SLAs.**

| Severity | Definition | Remediation SLA |
|---|---|---|
| Critical (CVSS 9.0–10.0) | Actively exploited or remote code execution |

| Critical (CVSS 9.0–10.0) | Actively exploited or unauthenticated remote code execution | 48 hours | Log4Shell, MOVEit-style zero-day |
| High (CVSS 7.0–8.9) | Significant exposure, likely exploitable, no active exploitation confirmed | 7 calendar days | Unpatched RDP, privilege escalation on domain controller |
| Medium (CVSS 4.0–6.9) | Exploitable under specific conditions, limited blast radius | 30 calendar days | Outdated TLS version, missing security headers |
| Low (CVSS 0.1–3.9) | Minimal risk, requires local access or chained exploitation | 90 calendar days | Informational misconfigurations, deprecated cipher suites |
| Informational | No direct risk, best-practice recommendation | Next scheduled maintenance window | Banner disclosure, verbose error messages |

Where a patch is unavailable from the vendor, a compensating control (network isolation, WAF rule, enhanced monitoring) must be documented and approved by the CISO within the same SLA window. The absence of a vendor patch does not pause the SLA clock.

**Escalation.** If a Critical or High vulnerability cannot be remediated within its SLA, the IT Lead must notify the CISO within 24 hours of the SLA breach. The CISO must notify the relevant business owner and, where customer data is at material risk, the Legal/Compliance team within a further 24 hours. All escalations must be logged in the risk register as a risk acceptance or treatment item.

**Exceptions.** Any exception to this policy (including SLA extensions) requires written approval from the CISO, must document the business justification and compensating controls in place, and must be reviewed every 30 days until resolved. Exceptions exceeding 90 days require sign-off from senior management. The exception log is reviewed at each management review meeting.

**Measurement.** The IT Lead produces a monthly vulnerability dashboard covering: total open findings by severity, SLA compliance rate, mean time to remediate by severity, and number of active exceptions. This report is provided to the CISO and tabled at the quarterly security review.

**Review.** This policy is reviewed annually or following a significant vulnerability incident, material change to the IT estate, or relevant regulatory guidance update.

This table overlays your existing ITIL incident process. Train your service desk, IT team, and SOC on the thresholds. The trigger column is what moves an event up to the next tier.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Security Event** | Any observable occurrence that may be relevant to information security but has not been confirmed as harmful or policy-violating | Failed login attempt (single), port scan detected by Splunk, phishing email caught by filter, automated alert with no confirmed impact | Log in SIEM. SOC reviews within SLA (per MDR contract). No ticket required unless escalated. | 5+ failed logins on privileged account within 10 min; alert confirmed as targeted; any anomaly on a Tier 1 asset | Escalate to Security Incident | No | SOC closes or escalates within 4 hours |
| **Security Incident** | A confirmed or highly probable violation of security policy, or an event that has caused or is likely to cause harm to information assets, systems, or individuals | Confirmed malware on endpoint, successful phishing leading to credential compromise, unauthorised access to customer data, unencrypted device lost, misconfigured Azure storage blob exposing data | Raise P2 ticket in ITSM. Notify IT Lead and CISO within 1 hour. Invoke IS incident procedure. Begin containment. Preserve evidence. | Customer data confirmed exposed; more than one system affected; attacker persistence suspected; IT Lead judges potential regulatory threshold met | Escalate to Major Incident. Notify Legal/Compliance immediately. | Possibly — Legal/Compliance assesses within 2 hours of escalation | Containment within 4 hours. Full post-incident review within 5 business days. |
| **Major Security Incident** | A security incident with confirmed or probable significant impact on customers, business operations, regulatory standing, or the organisation's ability to deliver services | Ransomware encrypting production systems, confirmed data breach involving 100+ customer records, prolonged system outage caused by attack, supply chain compromise affecting core platforms, insider threat with exfiltration confirmed | Invoke major incident process. CISO assumes incident commander. Convene crisis team (IT Lead, Legal, MGT, Comms). Isolate affected systems. Engage MDR/SOC on priority basis. | Regulation / body | Trigger | Notification deadline |

| UK FCA / PRA | Operational incident or data breach with material impact on services or customers | As soon as practicable; major incidents within 24 hours (operational resilience rules) |

| EU DORA (if applicable) | Major ICT-related incident | Initial notification within 4 hours of classification, no later than 24 hours |
| PCI DSS (if card data in scope) | Suspected or confirmed cardholder data compromise | Immediately to acquiring bank and card brands |

**A note on the "awareness" clock:** under GDPR and DORA, the notification clock starts when your organisation becomes aware of the incident, not when it is fully investigated. When in doubt, notify early and update. Legal should be looped in at the Security Incident tier at the latest.

## A Few Practical Notes Before You Paste

On the SoA, fill in every row even if the status is "Not started" — a blank cell looks worse to an auditor than an honest "planned with justification." On the incident rubric, share it with your outsourced SOC so their escalation thresholds match yours — a mismatch there is a common Stage 2 audit finding. On the supplier register, the right-to-audit column often surprises people: for major SaaS providers you typically won't get a direct audit right, but accepting their SOC 2 as equivalent is standard practice as long as the CISO documents that decision. And on the vulnerability policy, the exception log tends to grow quickly in the first year — build it into your monthly security review from day one so it doesn't become a graveyard of stale entries by the time your Stage 2 audit comes around.

## Access Control Policy

---

**Document title:** Access Control Policy
**Document reference:** POL-003
**Version:** 1.0
**Status:** Draft
**Owner:** IT Lead / CISO
**Approved by:** *(signature block at end)*
**Date issued:** [date]
**Next review date:** [date + 1 year]
**Classification:** Internal

---

**1. Purpose**

This policy defines how [Organisation Name] controls access to its information assets, systems, and data to ensure that access is granted on a need-to-know, least-privilege basis, is actively managed throughout the access lifecycle, and is reviewed regularly. It supports compliance with ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A controls 5.15, 5.16, 5.17, 5.18, 8.2, 8.3, and 8.5, and with applicable regulatory requirements including [UK FCA/PRA rules / GDPR — confirm with Legal].

---

**2. Scope**

This policy applies to all employees, contractors, third-party suppliers, and any other individuals accessing [Organisation Name] systems, applications, or data, whether on-premises, via Microsoft Azure, or via SaaS platforms including Microsoft 365 and Salesforce. It covers all access methods including corporate devices, remote access, and service accounts.

---

**3. Roles and Responsibilities**

| Role | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| CISO / Security Lead | Policy ownership, annual review, exception approval, privileged access oversight |
| IT Lead | Technical implementation, access provisioning and deprovisioning, access review execution, MFA enforcement |
| People / HR Manager | Triggering joiners/movers/leavers notifications, confirming role changes, maintaining employment records |
| Line Managers | Requesting access for their staff, approving access requests, confirming access is still required at review |
| All Users | Complying with this policy, not sharing credentials, reporting suspected unauthorised access immediately |
| Legal / Compliance | Advising on regulatory access obligations, reviewing access logs where required for investigations |

---

**4. Access Provisioning — Principles**

All access must be formally requested and approved before it is granted. Requests must specify the system, the level of access required, and the business justification. The IT Lead provisions access only on receipt of an approved request; verbal requests are not sufficient.

**Least privilege.** Users are granted the minimum level of access required to perform their role. Access to customer data, financial records, and systems classified Confidential or Restricted requires explicit business justification approved by the relevant line manager and, for Restricted data, the CISO.

**Need to know.** Access to sensitive data is restricted to individuals who require it to fulfil a specific, defined business function. Broad or department-wide access to sensitive data stores is not permitted without documented justification.

**Segregation of duties.** No single individual should have end-to-end control over a sensitive process. Where technically feasible, the person who requests a change should not be the same person who approves and implements it.

---

**5. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)**

Access to all systems must be managed through defined roles rather than individual permissions wherever technically possible. Azure Active Directory (Entra ID) groups and roles are the primary mechanism for RBAC enforcement across cloud and hybrid systems.

A role matrix must be maintained by the IT Lead, mapping job titles and functions to system roles and permission levels. The role matrix is reviewed as part of each access review cycle and updated within 5 business days of any role change. The current role matrix is maintained at [document location / SharePoint link].

Default access for new starters is defined per role in the role matrix. Any access beyond the default requires a separate approved access request.

---

**6. Privileged Access and Just-in-Time (JIT) Access**

Privileged access — including domain administrator, global administrator, subscription owner, and any role with the ability to modify security controls, access bulk customer data, or alter audit logs — is subject to the following controls in addition to standard access rules.

Privileged roles must not be used for routine day-to-day tasks. Individuals requiring privileged access must hold a separate privileged account distinct from their standard user account. Privileged accounts must not have mailboxes or be used for browsing or email.

Just-in-time access via Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management (PIM) is mandatory for all Azure and Microsoft 365 privileged roles. Activation requires business justification, is time-limited (maximum 8-hour sessions unless CISO-approved exception), and generates an audit log. Standing privileged access is not permitted for cloud roles except where technically unavoidable, in which case a documented exception approved by the CISO is required.

The number of privileged accounts must be kept to the minimum necessary. The IT Lead reviews the full list of privileged accounts monthly and reports exceptions to the CISO.

---

**7. Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)**

MFA is mandatory for all user accounts without exception. The following minimum standards apply.

| Access type | MFA requirement |
|---|---|
| All corporate users (standard) | MFA required for all authentication, enforced via Entra ID Conditional Access |
| Privileged / admin accounts | Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2 key or certificate-based) required |
| Remote access / VPN | MFA required as a condition of connection |
| SaaS platforms (O365, Salesforce) | MFA enforced at identity provider (Entra ID SSO) |
| Service accounts | MFA not applicable — mitigated by IP restriction, certificate auth, and no interactive login |
| Third-party / contractor access | MFA required; provisioned via guest account or approved remote access method only |

Exceptions to MFA requirements are not permitted without written CISO approval and a documented compensating control. MFA registration status is reviewed monthly by the IT Lead using the Entra ID MFA registration report.

---

**8. Joiners, Movers, and Leavers (JML)**

HR must notify the IT Lead of all starters, role changes, and leavers within the timelines below. The IT Lead is responsible for acting within the specified window.

| Event | HR notification | IT action required | SLA |
|---|---|---|---|
| New starter (joiner) | Before or on first day | Provision access per role matrix, enrol MFA, issue device | Same day as start |
| Role change (mover) | Before effective date | Adjust access to new role, remove access no longer required | Within 2 business days |
| Resignation / termination (leaver) | Immediately on confirmation | Disable account, revoke all sessions, remove from all groups | Within 2 hours for involuntary; end of last working day for voluntary |
| Contractor end of engagement | Before end date | As per leaver process | End of last day |
| Prolonged absence (>30 days) | When confirmed | Disable account for duration | Within 2 business days of confirmation |

Leavers' accounts must be disabled, not deleted, for a minimum of 30 days following departure to allow for investigation if required, then deleted in accordance with the Data Classification and Retention Policy.

---

**9. Access Reviews**

Formal access reviews must be conducted at the following cadence. All review outputs must be retained as evidence for a minimum of 3 years.

| Review type | Frequency | Owner | Method | Evidence retained |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| All-user access review | Quarterly | IT Lead | Entra ID access review (Identity Governance) | Exported review report, remediation log |
| Privileged account review | Monthly | IT Lead + CISO | Manual review of PIM role assignments | Review log, any removals documented |
| Service account review | Quarterly | IT Lead | Manual review of service principals and managed identities | Review log |
| SaaS platform review (Salesforce, O365) | Quarterly | IT Lead | Admin console user export, manager confirmation | Exported user list, manager sign-off emails |
| Supplier / third-party access review | Annually (or on contract change) | IT Lead + Legal | Review of active guest accounts and VPN credentials | Review log |

Where a review identifies access that is no longer required or appropriate, it must be removed within 5 business days of identification. Where removal is not immediately possible, it must be logged as an exception and approved by the CISO.

---

**10. Exceptions**

Any exception to this policy requires written approval from the CISO, must document the business justification and any compensating controls, and must be reviewed every 30 days. Exceptions are logged in the Policy Exception Register maintained by the CISO. Exceptions exceeding 90 days require sign-off from senior management.

---

**11. Non-Compliance**

Breach of this policy may result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal, in accordance with [Organisation Name]'s disciplinary procedure. Where a breach constitutes a criminal offence or regulatory violation, the matter will be referred to the appropriate authority.

---

**12. Related Documents**

Information Security Policy (POL-001) | Acceptable Use Policy (POL-002) | Data Classification Policy (POL-004) | Vulnerability Management Policy (POL-005) | Incident Management Policy (POL-006) | Supplier Security Policy (POL-007)

---

**13. Review and Sign-Off**

This policy is reviewed annually by the CISO or following any material change to the access control environment, a significant access-related incident, or relevant regulatory guidance update.

| Role | Name | Signature | Date |
|---|---|---|---|
| Policy Owner (CISO / IT Lead) | | | |
| Senior Management Sponsor | | | |
| Legal / Compliance Review | | | |

---

*Ready for the Data Classification Policy next — just say the word.*

## Data Classification Policy

---

**Document title:** Data Classification Policy
**Document reference:** POL-004
**Version:** 1.0
**Status:** Draft
**Owner:** CISO / Legal & Compliance
**Approved by:** *(signature block at end)*
**Date issued:** [date]
**Next review date:** [date + 1 year]
**Classification:** Internal

---

**1. Purpose**

This policy defines how [Organisation Name] classifies, handles, labels, retains, and disposes of information assets to ensure that data is protected proportionately to its sensitivity, regulatory weight, and business value. It supports compliance with ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A controls 5.9, 5.10, 5.12, 5.13, and 8.10, and with applicable regulatory obligations including UK GDPR, FCA data management rules, and PCI DSS where card data is in scope. All employees, contractors, and third parties handling [Organisation Name] data must comply with this policy.

---

**2. Scope**

This policy applies to all information assets owned or processed by [Organisation Name] in any format — digital or physical — including documents, emails, database records, system logs, configuration files, and verbal communications where they relate to classified information. It covers all environments within the ISMS scope: on-premises systems, Microsoft Azure, Microsoft 365, Salesforce, and any other SaaS platform processing organisational data.

---

**3. Classification Tiers**

[Organisation Name] uses four classification tiers. Every information asset must be assigned a classification at creation or first receipt. When in doubt, classify at the higher tier.

---

**Tier 1 — Public**

Information that has been approved for unrestricted external release and would cause no harm if disclosed to any audience.

*Examples:* Published marketing materials, press releases, job advertisements, publicly available product information, the organisation's website content.

*Default assumption:* Nothing is Public unless explicitly approved for external release by an authorised owner.

---

**Tier 2 — Internal**

Information intended for use within [Organisation Name] that is not sensitive but is not approved for external distribution. Disclosure would cause minor embarrassment or operational inconvenience but no material harm.

*Examples:* Internal process documentation, meeting agendas with no sensitive content, general staff communications, internal project plans not containing financial or personal data, IT asset lists with no security-sensitive detail.

---

**Tier 3 — Confidential**

Information that is sensitive, commercially valuable, or subject to contractual or regulatory protection. Unauthorised disclosure could cause financial loss, reputational damage, regulatory sanction, or harm to individuals.

*Examples:* Customer personal data (names, contact details, account references), employee records, financial reports not yet published, contracts and commercial agreements, audit findings, security policies and procedures, system architecture diagrams.

*This tier covers the majority of data processed in the normal course of business in a finance firm.*

---

**Tier 4 — Restricted**

The highest classification. Information whose unauthorised disclosure would cause severe harm to the organisation, its customers, or individuals — including regulatory breach, significant financial loss, criminal liability, or risk to personal safety.

*Examples:* Customer financial account credentials or payment card data, bulk personal data exports, cryptographic keys and certificates, privileged access credentials, active incident investigation records, merger and acquisition information, regulatory investigation correspondence, data subject access request responses containing third-party data.

---

**4. Handling Rules by Tier**

| Control | Public | Internal | Confidential | Restricted |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Access | Anyone | All staff | Need-to-know, role-based | Named individuals only, CISO approval for new access |
| Storage (digital) | Any approved system | Any corporate system | Encrypted storage only; no personal devices or unapproved cloud | Encrypted storage with access logging; Azure storage with private endpoint and no public blob access |
| Storage (physical) | No restriction | Locked away when unattended | Locked cabinet; clear desk enforced | Secure cabinet with restricted key access; logged in and out |
| Transmission (email) | Unrestricted | Internal email acceptable | Encrypted email or secure file transfer; no unencrypted external email | Encrypted channel only; explicit recipient approval required; no bulk export without CISO sign-off |
| Transmission (file share) | Public-facing systems permitted | Internal SharePoint / Teams | SharePoint with appropriate permissions; no personal cloud storage (Dropbox etc.) | Dedicated SharePoint site with restricted membership and audit logging enabled |
| Printing | Unrestricted | Permitted | Collect immediately from printer; do not leave unattended | Avoid printing; if essential, supervised printing only and secure disposal immediately after use |
| Disposal (digital) | Standard deletion | Standard deletion | Secure deletion per disposal procedure; confirm in asset register | Cryptographic erasure or verified secure wipe; documented and signed off by IT Lead |
| Disposal (physical) | Recycling | Cross-cut shredding | Cross-cut shredding or confidential waste contractor | Witnessed destruction; certificate of destruction retained |
| Sharing with third parties | Permitted | Permitted with manager approval | Permitted only under NDA or DPA; log the disclosure | CISO approval required; legal review recommended; log in supplier register |
| Incident notification if lost | Not required | Log internally | Notify IT Lead and CISO within 1 hour | Treat as security incident immediately; invoke incident procedure |

---

**5. Labelling**

All documents and files must carry a visible classification label. Use the standard labels below. In Microsoft 365, sensitivity labels must be applied using Microsoft Purview Information Protection (configured by IT Lead). Physical documents must be marked in the header and footer.

| Classification | Label text | Microsoft Purview label name | Physical document marking |
|---|---|---|---|
| Public | PUBLIC | Public | Header and footer: PUBLIC |
| Internal | INTERNAL | Internal | Header and footer: INTERNAL |
| Confidential | CONFIDENTIAL | Confidential | Header and footer: CONFIDENTIAL |
| Restricted | RESTRICTED — [reason, e.g., CUSTOMER DATA] | Restricted | Header and footer: RESTRICTED — [reason]; cover page required for multi-page documents |

Automated labelling policies in Microsoft Purview should be configured to detect and suggest labels for content containing personal data, financial account numbers, or payment card data. The IT Lead is responsible for maintaining the Purview label configuration.

---

**6. Labelling and Handling Examples by Platform**

**Salesforce records**

Customer account records in Salesforce containing name, contact details, and financial account references are classified **Confidential** by default. Records containing payment card numbers, authentication credentials, or bulk data exports are **Restricted**. Access must be provisioned via role-based profiles in Salesforce, aligned to the role matrix in the Access Control Policy. Salesforce reports or exports containing customer PII must not be saved to personal devices or unapproved storage. Any bulk export of customer records requires CISO approval and must be logged in the asset register as a data extract with a defined retention period and deletion date. Salesforce fields containing card data must be masked at display level and access-logged.

**SharePoint documents**

All SharePoint sites must have a designated owner responsible for access and classification. Documents must carry a Microsoft Purview sensitivity label matching their classification tier. SharePoint sites containing Confidential or Restricted content must have external sharing disabled, guest access blocked, and audit logging enabled. Documents auto-classified by Purview as containing personal data or financial information must be reviewed by the site owner within 10 business days and confirmed or reclassified. HR records, legal correspondence, and security documentation must be stored in dedicated SharePoint sites with restricted membership, not in general department sites. No Restricted documents should be stored in SharePoint without IT Lead confirmation that the site has the correct access controls and audit logging in place.

**Azure storage blobs**

All Azure storage accounts must be configured with public blob access disabled by default; this must be enforced via Azure Policy at the subscription level. Storage accounts containing Confidential or Restricted data must enable encryption at rest using Microsoft-managed keys as a minimum, with customer-managed keys (CMK) in Azure Key Vault required for Restricted data stores. Blob containers must be tagged with the data classification, data owner, and retention date using the organisation's standard Azure tagging policy. Access to storage accounts must be via private endpoints only for Confidential and Restricted tiers; no public endpoint exposure is permitted. Shared Access Signature (SAS) tokens for Confidential or Restricted storage must be time-limited (maximum 24 hours), scoped to the minimum required permissions, and their generation logged. Storage accounts must not use account-level access keys for application access; managed identities or service principals with RBAC are required.

---

**7. Retention and Deletion**

Information must be retained for the minimum period required by law, regulation, or business need, and deleted securely when that period expires. The table below gives standard retention periods for common data types in a finance firm. Legal must confirm these against your specific regulatory obligations before this policy is finalised.

| Data type | Classification | Minimum retention | Maximum retention | Deletion method |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Customer financial records | Confidential / Restricted | 6 years (FCA COBS / SYSC) | 7 years | Secure deletion; confirmed in asset register |
| Customer personal data (non-financial) | Confidential | Duration of relationship + 6 years | As above unless shorter purpose limitation applies | Secure deletion; subject access / erasure requests handled per GDPR procedure |
| Employee records | Confidential | Duration of employment + 6 years | 7 years post-employment | Secure deletion by HR, confirmed by IT Lead |
| Payment card data (if in scope) | Restricted | As short as possible; PCI DSS prohibits retention of sensitive authentication data post-authorisation | Do not retain beyond authorisation | Cryptographic erasure or verified secure wipe; certificate retained |
| Security logs and audit trails | Internal / Confidential | 12 months online (Splunk) | 7 years archived (regulatory requirement for finance) | Standard deletion from archive after retention period; IT Lead confirms |
| Contracts and legal agreements | Confidential | Duration + 7 years | 10 years for significant contracts | Secure deletion; legal sign-off before deletion |
| Incident records | Confidential | 3 years | 7 years if regulatory investigation involved | Secure deletion; CISO sign-off before deletion |
| Backup data | Varies (inherits source classification) | Per backup policy | Must not exceed retention period of source data | Cryptographic erasure on decommission; backup job deletion logs retained |
| System and application logs | Internal | 90 days online | 12 months; 7 years if subject to investigation hold | Standard deletion; IT Lead confirms |

**Deletion process.** When a retention period expires, the data owner is responsible for initiating deletion. The IT Lead confirms technical deletion and updates the asset register. For Restricted data, deletion must be witnessed or verified by a second person and recorded with date, method, and confirmation in the asset register. Deletion must not be deferred without a documented legal hold or CISO-approved exception.

**Legal holds.** Where data is subject to litigation, regulatory investigation, or a subject access request, normal retention and deletion schedules are suspended for the relevant data until Legal confirms the hold is lifted. Legal is responsible for notifying the IT Lead of holds and their removal.

---

**8. Responsibilities**

| Role | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| CISO | Policy ownership, annual review, exception approval, oversight of classification programme |
| IT Lead | Technical implementation of labelling tools, storage controls, deletion procedures, and Azure tagging policy |
| Legal / Compliance | Confirming regulatory retention requirements, managing legal holds, reviewing third-party data sharing |
| Data Owners (business leads) | Assigning classification to assets they own, reviewing and confirming labels annually, approving access requests |
| All Staff | Applying correct labels at creation, handling data per tier rules, reporting suspected misclassification or data loss immediately |
| HR | Applying policy to employee records, triggering deletion on leaver process completion |

---

**9. Exceptions**

Any exception to handling or retention rules requires written approval from the CISO, must document the justification and risk, and is reviewed every 30 days. Exceptions are logged in the Policy Exception Register. Exceptions involving Restricted data or regulatory retention requirements must also be reviewed by Legal.

---

**10. Related Documents**

Information Security Policy (POL-001) | Acceptable Use Policy (POL-002) | Access Control Policy (POL-003) | Supplier Security Policy (POL-007) | Incident Management Policy (POL-006) | Asset Register | Microsoft Purview Label Configuration Guide (IT-DOC-012)

---

**11. Review and Sign-Off**

This policy is reviewed annually by the CISO and Legal, or following a data classification-related incident, a material change to the data environment, or relevant regulatory or legislative update.

| Role | Name | Signature | Date |
|---|---|---|---|
| Policy Owner (CISO) | | | |
| Legal / Compliance Review | | | |
| Senior Management Sponsor | | | |

---

You now have five of the twelve core Phase 1 policies drafted and paste-ready: the Vulnerability Management Policy, Access Control Policy, and Data Classification Policy as full documents, plus the Incident Management overlay and Supplier Security framework as working templates.
